clips.title: Why I Read My Agent Session Logs, Not Just the Output

lines.text: Most people just analyze the output of their sessions when they're dealing with agents. I analyze the output of the
entire session history. So, something that I've learned after dealing with agents for the past 6 months is or longer, however long agents have been
around, is that the session logs are super important to learning and knowing what to do and knowing how to change.
And a lot of these session logs are stored right on your computer. So, what I do is at the end of all my sessions, or actually every 15 minutes, I think, I
back up all of my session logs from all of my sessions, from all of my computers where it's running, and then I go through them weekly, monthly,
every 3 months, and basically can start to run experiments or start to see has the agents completed more work? Has
the agents been fanning out? Has the agents been following my rules? Or start to see the drift. And I can start to see where I move from one model to the next.
So, right now I'm mainly working in Codex, and I've switched over to Google Gemini and a little bit of Claude.
Uh and and Kimmy. 2 months ago, it was all Claude, uh no Kimmy, right? And and because I store all of my session logs, you can see the outputs and the actions
from each one. I highly recommend doing that and running through your session logs, and this is my favorite loop from it is I ask it what tasks did we not
accomplish that we should have accomplished or that we can make rules for. I also tell it to look up every time I've ever cursed at it, and
uh create rules to put into my hooks and harnesses to stop that from happening again. Hopefully, it sometimes works, it sometimes doesn't. It's a It's a
learning process. And then my also favorite one is untracked or kind of like
um lost threads. So, about once a month or I have it go through and look for all the lost threads. So, because I have so
many chat sessions open, I might go look for ones where I started a chat and then forgot to finish it. Um I have ones that happen weekly for actual work, but these
are more of the experimental ones, the fun ideas that I had. And then I'll have it go maybe close thread, maybe I'll restart the project, but it's a fun way
of kind of keeping track and then even if you're maxed out thinking-wise, you can always circle back because you
literally have a notebook of every conversation you've ever said to an AI agent. So, just keep that in mind.
Follow my link for more.

clips.title: Context rot is why your coding agent keeps choking

lines.text: I build agents and I build a lot of them for businesses. So, if your coding agent keeps choking mid-task, it's definitely
not your GPU, the model, or it's most likely context rot. So, everyone thinks that having a bigger context is just
more memory, but sometimes it's not. So, Chroma had tested 18 frontier models and found that every single one started
hallucinating, ignoring rules, and then dropping details before the window was even half full, and you'll hear this all around people saying this. I know I
experienced it. And here's what I run to fix this problem. So, when most people build agents, they dump 100,000 tokens
of logs, rules, chat history into your Claude MD, and you're going to assume that the model reads it all. One, it definitely doesn't even need that anymore. The newest updates to Claude
make it more goal-focused than needing a rule-focused, and we'll get into that in another video. But, when you give it
that much in the beginning, its attention starts to really spread thin, and the model will start to skim its own history and kind of guess what to do
next, and that's never really what you want to do. Here's the next bug that happens. So, whenever you switch the chat or compact
the chat, something sometimes conversation gets lost or when you clear the chat, then your session start might
not refire, which if you have rules in your session start hooks and they're not firing, well, that could be part of the reason why your agent's not behaving. I
had that happen to me for like, I don't know, 2 months before I realized that /clear didn't didn't actually like reset it. I don't know if they've changed that
since then because I no longer do that. Um so, anyways, the the fix is really simple for most this.
You're going to stop putting the rules into static suggestion files and just move them into deterministic execution hooks. So, you want to reinject on every
prompt. So, I have a hook that reinjects the project boundaries, the host maps, and some live data on every single turn.
People argue that that's not the best use of it, but I don't really care. It works for me. Um pre-compaction checkpoint, so right before the context
switches, um my agent writes a one-line checkpoint with its objective and then the next step and maybe some other details. I
know other people pre-compact it and then push it over.
And then, um I have it always read the disk um or read the code. So, just literally, if your agent needs to
know what a function state does, um
yeah. So, if if your agent doesn't know what the function does, just have it reread it. So, it's a better than relying on something from 20 turns ago.
Um so, I rolled this So, I rolled this hook architecture
across 20 of my repos and 16 had these chronic chronic drift issues and then all of them stopped derailing after I
implemented this. Um and now I mainly run my loops hands-free end-to-end, which is really great. Um I also go through this monthly
um to to basically fix any of the issues.

clips.title: clean, fast-paced direct delivery

lines.text: I have built and open-sourced over 21 personal AI systems. And when developers ask me whether to build on retail Zapier Blend, they're all generally asking the
wrong questions. So, most people are going to obsess over voice latency, but latency is kind of solved, especially like you have Grok, you have Flash, you
have all these other ones. I think the hardest problem that most people have in voice AI, and 90% of voice agents die in production, is what I call the
transcript execution boundary. When a real human calls at 8:00 p.m., they don't speak in clean JSON, they ramble, they contradict themselves, and they
might give half a phone number and a cough. If your bot tries to push the live LM tool calls directly into the CRM during the phone call, your database
might get corrupted, your tool might drop, like everything can break. I know, I've tried, I've had things break. So, to fix this, I personally built an
asynchronous buffer, so that way the voice loop can stay completely decoupled from the data layer, and the moment the call dis- disconnects, a deterministic
state machine can validate the schema and process the action. We also have like action gateways and other approval engines built in, but that's a whole
story for another day. So, 12 seconds of human ran- rambling can become structured CRM operations in under 500
milliseconds milliseconds without anyone touching the keyboard. I've open-sourced the entire architecture on my GitHub today. So, go check it out. You
can go inspect it at cgalleg.github.io/cgalleg-stack.
